title: Beyond the Symptom Score: What Standard Psychiatric Rating Scales Fail to Capture — A Narrative Review
content: Standard psychiatric rating scales such as the PANSS, HAM-D and MADRS remain the dominant outcome measures in clinical trials and routine care, yet they were built to quantify symptom severity rather than to register the full range of change that matters to patients. This narrative review synthesized psychometric, validation, epidemiological and trial evidence, together with consensus reports, to identify clinically and personally meaningful improvements that symptom-focused scales fail to detect. Evidence converged on ten under-measured outcome domains: real-world functioning, which correlates only weakly with symptoms and often lags behind them; cognition and social cognition; negative symptoms and motivational anhedonia; the subjective experience of medication; quality of life and positive mental health; personal recovery (connectedness, hope, identity, meaning and empowerment); internalized stigma; physical health and premature mortality, with all-cause mortality two to three-and-a-half times that of the general population; sleep and circadian function; and shared decision-making as a process outcome of care. Two cross-cutting limitations compound these gaps: systematic discordance among clinician, self-report and informant ratings, and the inability of retrospective, clinic-based instruments to capture the momentary, context-dependent dynamics now accessible through ecological momentary assessment and passive sensing. We propose a pragmatic, tiered outcome set that pairs every symptom scale with measures of functioning and of quality of life or recovery, adds physical health, sleep and medication burden, and reserves digital methods for settings that can support them. Improvement in psychiatry is multidimensional; measuring it as such is a scientific necessity, not a refinement.
